newsitem.title: GERMANY: Growing signs German tax receipts are below target.
newsitem.headline: Growing signs German tax receipts are below target.

text.p: New data from regional states on Wednesday showed that tax revenues so far this year have come in well below expectations, endangering Germany's bid to qualify for Europe's planned single currency.

Financial markets are eagerly awaiting the data due next month on first quarter federal tax receipts and Bonn's forecast for the full year in order to determine what chances Germany has of meeting the fiscal targets for monetary union.

Doubts about Bonn's ability to keep its budget deficit from exceeding three percent, as required by the Maastricht treaty, has fuelled speculation that European economic and monetary union (EMU) would be delayed if Bonn failed to qualify.

With publication of tax data for the first three months of 1997 by several regional states, it now appears that Finance Minister Theo Waigel is under increasing pressure to offset sharply falling tax revenues.
The southwestern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg, one of Germany's four most-populous states, said tax receipts in the first quarter of the year were more than 10 percent lower than expected.
"Tax receipts across the country in the first quarter of 1997 have remained well below expectations," Baden-Wuerttemberg finance minister Gerhard Mayer-Vorfelder said in a statement.

In Bavaria, officials said first quarter tax revenues were 8.4 percent below budget, a decline of 5.5 percent from the same period a year ago. In North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state, tax revenues fell 6.4 percent from a year ago, while in Hesse tax income fell 6.5 percent.
In Chancellor Helmut Kohl's home state Rhineland Palatinate tax receipts fell 11 percent and in Lower Saxony tax revenues were down 0.7 percent.
"If tax revenues do not improve sharply then it could become very difficult for Maastricht," a Lower Saxony finance ministry spokesman said.

State officials said there were some signs of hope. Tax receipts in March were generally better than in the two months before and later in the year tax increases on inheritance and property purchase would kick in.

The Bonn Finance Ministry declined comment on the state figures. It said there were no federal data available yet for the first quarter, but that tax receipts were down 5.5 percent in January and February from the same two months a year ago.
The ministry cited special technical factors that distorted the January and February data and added that it could not make a reliable evaluation until the next tax estimate in May.

Meanwhile, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said the economy probably grew slightly in the first quarter but that economic expansion would have to accelerate in order to meet the government's forecast of 2.5 percent growth this year.
